findings.claim: “essential for the Eduqas C720U exam, where AO4 (context) runs through both Part (i) and Part (ii) of the Shakespeare question”
findings.truth: AO4 in this section is spelling, punctuation and grammar. The Shakespeare section assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 only, so context is not a credited objective. The board must also not be named in student-facing text.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md: ‘Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4.’

findings.claim: “Part (i) gives you a printed extract worth 20 marks and Part (ii) ... another 20 marks. Context (AO4) must be embedded...”
findings.truth: AO4 is written accuracy, not context. The spec gives Section A as 40 marks through one extract-based question and one whole-text essay, but states no per-question split, so the 20 + 20 numbers are removed.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1 Component 1 Section A (40 marks); 'Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4.'

findings.claim: “She speaks only 42 lines in the first three acts” (repeated in lesson 6 content and flashcard 9)
findings.truth: Hero speaks roughly 95 lines (about 760 words) in Acts 1-3, most of them in Act 3 where she leads the gulling of Beatrice. She is near-silent only in Acts 1-2.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/much-ado.txt, counted across all HERO speeches to the end of Act 3.

findings.claim: Every practice question in all 8 lessons is labelled ‘[20]’ and typed “20 marks — Extract Analysis” / “20 marks — Wider Text Response”.
findings.truth: The spec states 40 marks for the section but no per-question split, so 20 + 20 is unverifiable. Left in place rather than re-labelled across 48 questions; flagged for a fleet decision.

findings.claim: “they never meet but there’s a skirmish of wit betwixt them”
findings.truth: Leonato says ‘skirmish of wit between them’. ‘Betwixt’ belongs to the earlier clause, ‘a kind of merry war betwixt Signior Benedick and her’.

findings.claim: “Explores AO4 context on bastardy in Elizabethan society.”
findings.truth: AO4 is written accuracy. Context is not a credited objective on the Shakespeare question, so a mark scheme that awards it under AO4 misdirects the student.
findings.evidence: spec: 'Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4.'

findings.claim: In the gulling of Benedick the men say Beatrice is “desperately” in love and “so possessed with a fury” of affection.
findings.truth: Neither phrase is in Act 2, Scene 3. ‘Possessed with a fury’ is Benedick about Beatrice in Act 1, Scene 1. ‘Desperately’ does not occur. The scene's wording is Leonato's ‘enraged affection’ and ‘a desperate outrage to herself’.
findings.evidence: much-ado.txt line 428 (Act 1, Scene 1); lines 1626 and 1709-1710 (Act 2, Scene 3).

findings.claim: “In Act 3, Scene 3, Don John stages a scene at Hero’s window” and “Borachio describes the plan” there.
findings.truth: Borachio lays the plan in Act 2, Scene 2. The deception itself happens off-stage the night before the wedding, and Act 3, Scene 3 is Borachio boasting to Conrade that it is already done.
findings.evidence: much-ado.txt line 1443 (Act 2, Scene 2 plan); line 2512 (Act 3, Scene 3, 'I have tonight wooed Margaret').

findings.claim: “write me down an ass” is taught as a Dogberry malapropism (lesson 3 and lesson 6 definitions, lesson 7 prose, lesson 7 knowledge check 4).
findings.truth: It is not a malapropism. Dogberry uses the word correctly and demands the insult be recorded; the comedy is that it fits him. His real malapropisms include 'odorous' for 'odious'.

findings.claim: “the most likely extract for the Eduqas exam ... link it to the patriarchal honour code (AO4)”
findings.truth: AO4 is written accuracy, not context, and the board must not be named in student-facing text.
findings.evidence: spec: 'Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4.'

findings.claim: “AO4 on women’s lack of agency.”
findings.truth: AO4 is written accuracy; context is not credited on this question.
findings.evidence: spec: 'Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4.'

findings.claim: At the double wedding “Benedick declares ‘I do love nothing in the world so well as you — is not that strange?’”
findings.truth: That declaration is Act 4, Scene 1, in the church after the shaming, not Act 5, Scene 4. A student citing it as part of the ending would place a key quotation in the wrong scene.

findings.claim: “Benedick’s final line — ‘man is a giddy thing, and this is my conclusion’” (also lesson 6)
findings.truth: He speaks several times after it. His last words, and the play's, are 'Strike up, pipers!'

findings.claim: “For the Eduqas exam, this line is a strong conclusion...”
findings.truth: House rule: Eduqas lessons never name the board in student-facing text.

findings.claim: “Leonato hints that Beatrice was once hurt by Benedick (‘she hath been ever an hour with the Prince’s fool’)”
findings.truth: The quotation does not exist in the play, and the hint is Beatrice's own, in Act 2, Scene 1: Benedick 'won it of me with false dice'.
findings.evidence: much-ado.txt lines 1222-1223; no match anywhere for 'hath been ever an hour'.

findings.claim: “Always link character to theme (AO1/AO2) and context (AO4).”
findings.truth: AO4 is written accuracy; context is not assessed on the Shakespeare question.

findings.claim: Extract set ‘from “O that I were a man for his sake!” to “I would eat his heart in the marketplace”’.
findings.truth: The range runs backwards: 'eat his heart in the market-place' comes about twenty lines before 'O that I were a man for his sake'. Start point re-pointed to 'Is he not approved in the height a villain'.

findings.claim: “Beatrice’s ‘She speaks poniards, and every word stabs’”
findings.truth: The line is Benedick's, spoken about Beatrice in Act 2, Scene 1. Lesson 2 attributes it correctly; lesson 7 gives it to Beatrice.

findings.claim: “a key AO2 tool for the Eduqas exam” and “For the Eduqas exam (AO2)”
findings.truth: House rule: never name the board in student-facing text.

findings.truth: The Shakespeare section assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 only. AO3 is not assessed at all, and AO4 is spelling, punctuation and grammar, not context.

findings.truth: Same AO4 error, in the one place a student is shown how to write a paragraph. Labels removed and the paragraph re-framed as analysis plus supporting context.

findings.truth: The keyed answer (AO1, AO2 and AO4) is right; only the board name is removed.

findings.claim: “The Eduqas C720U Shakespeare question has two parts: Part (i) is worth _____ marks ... and Part (ii) is worth the same”, keyed to 20.
findings.truth: The spec states no per-question split, so the keyed answer is unverifiable and drills a number the board does not publish. Re-pointed at the 40-mark section total, which the spec does state; the keyed index 2 stays correct.

findings.claim: “Part (i) 20-mark extract, Part (ii) 20-mark whole text”, plus two board-naming prompts and “How should AO4 context be embedded”.
findings.truth: Unverifiable split replaced with the 40-mark total; board name removed; AO4 is written accuracy, not context.

findings.truth: The closed-book claim is correct; the board name and spec code must go.

summary: Every lesson carried at least one error. The dominant fault is a board-wide AO mislabel: AO4 is taught as context in six lessons, and lesson 8 adds AO3, when the Shakespeare section assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 (written accuracy) only and gives no marks for context. Also found one fabricated quotation, three misattributed or misplaced quotations, a wrong scene for the window plot, a backwards extract range, a false line-count statistic, and eight places that name the board in student-facing text.
